question: Does a data-driven classification of neuropsychological test scores agree with the clinical consensus diagnosis of MCI versus normal cognition in non-demented Alzheimer's Disease Research Center participants? P-955 answers it for LCA in one ADRC (Penn), P-1084 for Ward hierarchical clustering across 46 NACC ADRCs. The population class (non-demented ADRC older adults) and the channel (neuropsychological test scores) are the same. P-1084 itself sets its result against P-955 ('differs from a previous study that found 90% concordance').
metric: Agreement between data-driven and consensus MCI/NC classification: concordance proportion (with kappa, and the data-driven MCI share against the consensus MCI share). P-955 prints concordance and kappa. For P-1084 both are derived from its printed cross-tabulation (Table 2).

figures.P-955: Consensus against LCA: concordant for 90% of 354 participants, kappa 0.80 (printed). Wilson 95% CI for 0.90, n = 354: 0.864 to 0.927. LCA MCI 41% against consensus MCI 44% (3 points fewer). With race-adjusted norms: kappa 0.79, LCA MCI 44%. The actuarial Jak/Bondi rule (two scores > 1 SD below the norm in a domain, the impairment pattern of P-1084's cluster-MCI groups) against consensus: kappa 0.68; discordant 13% + 3%, so concordance 84%, Wilson 0.798 to 0.875.
figures.P-1084: Table 2, restricted to consensus NC (16,005) and consensus MCI (8,513) to match P-955's NC/MCI-only sample (the impaired-not-MCI column is dropped). Concordant = NC in cluster oCN/tCN (3081 + 5797 = 8,878) + MCI in cluster aMCI/mMCI (8513 - 232 - 1115 = 7,166) = 16,044 / 24,518 = 0.654, Wilson 0.648 to 0.660. Kappa: p_e = (16005/24518)(10225/24518) + (8513/24518)(14293/24518) = 0.6528 x 0.4170 + 0.3472 x 0.5830 = 0.4746, so kappa = (0.6544 - 0.4746)/(1 - 0.4746) = 0.342 (approximate SE 0.006, CI 0.331 to 0.353). Cluster MCI 58.3% against consensus MCI 34.7% in this subset, 23.6 points more (printed for the whole sample: 58.8% against 32.4% plus 6.6% impaired-not-MCI).
figures.difference: Concordance 0.90 [0.864, 0.927] against 0.654 [0.648, 0.660]: each estimate lies far outside the other's interval. Kappa 0.80 against 0.34. The data-driven method gives 3 points fewer MCI than consensus in P-955 and about 24 points more in P-1084. P-955's actuarial rule, the closest in impairment definition, still gives 84% [0.798, 0.875], also outside P-1084's interval.

matched_figure_check: No matched figure reconciles the pair. P-1084 prints no analysis with published (non-robust) demographic norms, with LCA, or within a single ADRC. P-955 prints no analysis with robust-CN norms. The nearest checks both leave the gap open. P-955's change of normative reference (adding race adjustment) leaves consensus-LCA agreement unchanged (0.79 against 0.80). Its actuarial two-scores-below-1-SD rule, which mirrors P-1084's cluster-MCI impairment pattern, still agrees with consensus at 84%.
performance_validity: Not a performance comparison (agreement between classification methods; no trained predictive model).

candidate_explanations.difference: Normative reference: robust-CN regression norms in P-1084 against published age/education/sex norms in P-955. P-1084 argues that robust norms raise the bar for 'normal'.
candidate_explanations.quote: While both studies leveraged demographically-adjusted neuropsychological z scores, only the current study derived z scores from the performance of robust cognitively normal participants.

candidate_explanations.difference: Same point, stated as a mechanism by P-1084 (not tested in either paper).
candidate_explanations.quote: Robust norms may create a higher standard for “normal” and thus identify more individuals as falling into an MCI group.

candidate_explanations.difference: Cohort and sampling frame: one ADRC (Penn, 44% consensus MCI) against the multi-site NACC UDS (32.4% consensus MCI).
candidate_explanations.quote: Additionally, the previous study was conducted in a sample of participants from one ADRC while we used the larger NACC UDS sample.

candidate_explanations.difference: How the consensus label is made: in NACC the consensus tracks global CDR and the subjective-complaint requirement, so people with low test scores but no reported complaint stay 'normal'.
candidate_explanations.quote: Consensus diagnoses closely corresponded to global CDR scores, which likely explains the considerable discrepancy between diagnostic methods.

candidate_explanations.difference: Impairment threshold implied by the cluster-MCI groups (two memory scores at least 1 SD below the mean) against conventional single-score 1.5 SD impairment.
candidate_explanations.quote: This difference in the definition of what constitutes memory impairment may have contributed to more participants being classified with MCI using our data-driven approach.

candidate_explanations.difference: Algorithm and input representation: LCA on six domain means (P-955) against Ward hierarchical clustering on individual test z-scores (P-1084).
candidate_explanations.quote: Cognitive domain scores, rather than individual test scores, were entered as indicators in LCA to ensure sufficient statistical power.

candidate_explanations.difference: Battery: 14 measures including CERAD word list and praxis (P-955) against a UDS subset of memory, digit/number span, TMT, category fluency and naming (P-1084).
candidate_explanations.quote: All participants completed the Uniform Data Set prescribed by the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center and additional cognitive tests.

reason: Both papers measure how well a data-driven neuropsychological classification agrees with consensus MCI diagnosis in ADRC participants. The agreement differs far beyond uncertainty: 90% (0.864 to 0.927, kappa 0.80) in P-955 against 65.4% (0.648 to 0.660, kappa 0.34), derived from P-1084's own cross-tabulation restricted to consensus NC and MCI. P-1084 names the difference from P-955 and offers explanations (robust-CN norms, a single ADRC against NACC, CDR-driven consensus, the impairment threshold). Neither paper tests any of them, so they are candidate explanations not shown to be sufficient. One caveat on independence, which the rule does not require: Penn ADRC contributes to NACC, so some P-955 participants are plausibly inside P-1084's sample. That makes the gap a difference of method more than of population.

quotes.quote: MCI rates by consensus, actuarial criteria, and LCA were 44%, 53%, and 41%, respectively.
Consensus and LCA diagnoses of MCI demonstrated substantial agreement, with concordant diagnoses for 90% of cases.

Thirteen percent of participants were classified as having MCI by actuarial criteria but NC by consensus (termed the “discrepant group” in subsequent analyses), while only 3% of participants were classified as having NC by actuarial criteria but MCI by consensus.

The agreement of the actuarial approach with consensus (0.72 versus 0.68) and with LCA (0.75 versus 0.70) improved slightly, while the agreement of consensus with LCA was unchanged (0.79 versus 0.80).
4) clinical consensus diagnosis of normal cognition (NC) or MCI at baseline. Participants with any other primary baseline diagnosis were excluded.

Overall, the cluster analysis classified a greater number of individuals as having MCI (58.8% of the sample) than did the consensus method (32.4% of the sample with MCI, plus another 6.6% impaired-not-MCI). Within NACC's MCI cohort, 84.2% were also classified into one of the cluster-derived MCI groups. However, only 55.5% of NACC's “normal cognition” cohort were classified into one of the cluster-derived CN groups

The current finding of a discrepancy between the cluster-derived classifications and consensus diagnoses differs from a previous study23 that found 90% concordance between statistically-determined MCI diagnoses from a latent profile analysis and consensus diagnoses.
Cluster analysis of baseline neuropsychological data was conducted by entering z scores into a hierarchical cluster analysis using the Ward method
